questions.q: What is the core structural difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?
options: An IAM user has no credentials of its own; a role always has a permanent access key
A role has no permanent credentials of its own and is assumed via sts:AssumeRole to get temporary credentials, while a user has long-lived credentials that don't expire on their own
IAM users can only be used by humans, while roles can only be used by AWS services
Roles are only usable for console access, never for programmatic API calls
questions.explain: An IAM user holds long-lived credentials (a password and/or access keys) that remain valid until rotated or deleted. A role has no credentials at all — principals assume it to receive temporary security credentials with a defined expiration.

questions.q: What question does a role's trust policy answer, as distinct from its permissions policy?
options: Who is allowed to assume this role, which is separate from what the role is allowed to do once assumed
How many API calls the role can make per second
Which AWS region the role is allowed to operate in
What encryption algorithm temporary credentials use
questions.explain: The trust policy (assume-role policy document) defines who can assume the role. The separate permissions policy defines what the role can actually do once assumed — the two answer different questions.

questions.q: Why does AWS recommend an EC2 instance profile or Lambda execution role over embedding an IAM user's access key in application config?
options: Instance profiles and execution roles are faster to provision than access keys
Embedded access keys are automatically encrypted by AWS, while role credentials are not
The compute service assumes the role on the workload's behalf and supplies temporary, auto-rotating credentials, so there's no long-lived key on disk or in deployment artifacts to leak
Access keys cannot be used at all by EC2 instances or Lambda functions
questions.explain: With an instance profile or execution role attached, the workload's SDK picks up temporary credentials automatically from the metadata service or execution environment — nothing long-lived ever needs to be stored or leaked.

questions.q: What is AWS IAM Identity Center's role in managing human access, as described in this lesson?
options: It federates workforce identity from an IdP into temporary, role-based access per account, replacing standing IAM users as the default way people sign in
It is a tool exclusively for managing EC2 instance profiles
It replaces the need for any IAM role trust policy
It is only used for encrypting access keys at rest
questions.explain: IAM Identity Center federates an identity provider into temporary, role-based sessions across accounts in an Organization, so humans get short-lived credentials per session instead of a standing IAM user.

questions.q: If a long-lived access key truly cannot be avoided, what does this lesson recommend to keep that risk manageable?
options: Storing the key in as many deployment artifacts as possible so it's easy to recover if lost
Disabling MFA on the IAM user so automated scripts can rotate it without prompts
Rotating it on a defined schedule, scoping its permissions tightly, and periodically pulling the IAM credential report to verify how old every key actually is
Attaching the FullAWSAccess SCP so the key's permissions are maximized
questions.explain: When a long-lived key is unavoidable, the practical mitigations are scheduled rotation, tight scoping, and using aws iam generate-credential-report to actually verify ages rather than just assuming rotation is happening.
